**Peach**

Would you care to hurl a stone at me?
Here—take all that remains of my peach.
Blood-red, and deep: Heaven alone knows how it came to be.
Someone's pound of flesh surrendered up,
Wrinkled with secrets,
And hardened with the resolve to keep them.

Why, from silvery peach-blossom,
From that shallow, silvered wine-glass poised upon a slender stem,
This rolling, falling, weighty globe?

I am musing, naturally, upon the peach as it was before I ate it.

Why so velvety, why so voluptuously heavy?
Why does it hang with such extravagant weight?
Why so deeply indented?
Why the groove?
Why these lovely, bivalve roundnesses?
Why the ripple coursing down the sphere?
Why the intimation of an incision?

Why was my peach not round and flawless, like a billiard ball?
It surely would have been, had man been its maker.

Though I have eaten it now.

Yet it was not round and finished like a billiard ball;
And because I dare to say so, you would like to fling something at me.

Here—you may have my peach stone.

*San Gervasio*
outputs.L2:
Do you feel the urge to hurl a rock in my direction? Go ahead, here—accept what remains of my peach. A profound crimson shade: only Heaven understands how this came to be. Someone's flesh surrendered up. Creased with hidden things and firm with the resolve to guard them. How strange—from delicate peach blossom, from that low silvery goblet perched atop its slender stem, comes this tumbling, sinking, weighty little sphere?

Naturally, my mind dwells on the peach as it was before I consumed it. What made it so soft to the touch, so richly and sensuously heavy? What caused it to dangle with such excessive heft? What formed those dimples and that furrow? Why the gorgeous, twin-shelled curves? Why does that wave run along its globe? What hints at a cut carved into it?

Why couldn't my peach have been smooth and complete like a billiard ball? That's precisely what it would have become had human hands crafted it. And yes, I have eaten it by now. Yet it was never smooth and complete like a billiard ball—and simply because I point this out, you'd want to fling something my way.

Here then—the peach stone is yours to keep.

San Gervasio
outputs.L3:
# On Offering a Peach Stone

Here, then—take what remains. I hold out to you the leftover stone of the peach I have eaten, and I offer it precisely to you, the one who bristles at my presence, who regards me with something close to hostility. Let this be our dialogue, then: not a gentle exchange, but a provocation, a gesture that dares you to consider what I have savored and what you have perhaps overlooked.

Consider the peach itself. It was blood-red and heavy in the hand, voluptuous in its ripeness, swollen with a richness that seemed almost extravagant. And yet think of its origins—how strange that such lush, sensual weight should have descended from a blossom so delicate, so pale and silvery, so easily scattered by the wind. From that fragile flowering came this dense and glowing fruit, and the contrast alone is enough to stir wonder.

But it is the form of the peach that most delights me. I marvel at its irregularities—the deep groove that runs along its side, the curious indentations, the subtle ripples across its skin, the way it rounds itself into two swelling halves like a bivalve shell. Nothing about it is uniform; nothing is mechanically precise. Its beauty lies entirely in these natural imperfections, in the organic asymmetry that no two peaches ever quite repeat.

Imagine, by contrast, if man had been the maker of the peach. Had human hands and human industry produced it, it would have emerged perfectly round, polished, smooth and finished—flawless as a billiard ball, and just as lifeless. It would possess symmetry, yes, but none of the wild grace that nature bestows. Manufacture would have stripped it of its soul, leaving only sterile precision where now there is living beauty.

And this, I suspect, is the very heart of what provokes you. It is my celebration of nature's rough and organic forms—my preference for the crooked over the straight, the irregular over the uniform, the naturally imperfect over the artificially complete—that rouses your antagonism. You would have order and finish; I find my delight in the uneven and the alive. So take the stone. Let it stand as the small, hard emblem of everything that divides us.

# On D.H. Lawrence's "Peach"

D.H. Lawrence's poem "Peach" transforms an ordinary act—eating a piece of fruit—into a sensuous meditation on the nature of beauty, provocation, and the tension between the natural and the artificial. What begins as a simple observation becomes a philosophical challenge directed at the reader, one that celebrates the messy, organic imperfection of the living world.

## The Sensual Form of the Peach

At the heart of the poem lies the speaker's tactile and visual fascination with the peach itself. He dwells upon its physical qualities with an almost erotic attentiveness: the soft curves of its body, the distinctive groove that runs along its surface, and the heavy, voluptuous weight of it resting in the hand. This is no ordinary description of a piece of fruit. Lawrence renders the peach as something almost bodily, its form evoking the sensual contours of flesh. The fruit's rounded fullness, its cleft and dimple, its yielding softness—all of these details invite the reader to consider the peach not as a mere object of consumption, but as a marvel of natural design, shaped by forces beyond human control.

## Nature Versus Artificial Perfection

The poem's central movement comes through a deliberate contrast. The speaker sets the irregular, imperfect peach against the flawless symmetry of a man-made billiard ball—an object of manufactured precision, perfectly round, uniform, and sterile. Why, the poem implicitly asks, is the peach not shaped like this? Why does nature refuse to produce something so clean and geometrically perfect?

The answer, the speaker suggests, is precisely the point. The peach's beauty lies in its irregularity, its unpredictable curves and mysterious complexity. The billiard ball, by comparison, represents a cold and lifeless kind of order—the sort of perfection that can only be achieved through human manufacture and that, in its very flawlessness, is drained of vitality and wonder. Nature does not deal in such tidy uniformity; instead, it produces forms that are organic, strange, and endlessly varied.

## The Provocation of the Reader

What gives the poem its characteristic Lawrentian edge is its confrontational tone. The speaker does not merely admire the peach; he uses it to challenge and provoke his audience. There is a sense that appreciating the untidy, sensual splendor of the peach is an act of rebellion—a defiance against those who would prefer the world to be sterile, controlled, and mechanically ordered. The reader who recoils from the fruit's messy vitality, who would rather have the neat perfection of the billiard ball, becomes the target of the speaker's provocation.

In this way, the poem transforms into a small manifesto for a way of seeing and living. To love the peach—with all its irregularity, its overflowing juice, its imperfect and voluptuous form—is to embrace the mystery and abundance of the natural world. To reject it in favor of manufactured order is to align oneself with sterility and lifelessness.

## Conclusion

Through his meditation on a single piece of fruit, Lawrence celebrates nature's refusal to conform to human ideals of perfection. The peach becomes a symbol of organic beauty, sensual richness, and the wild, unpredictable creativity of the natural world. In championing the imperfect over the flawless, the living over the manufactured, the poem invites us to take pleasure in irregularity itself—and it dares us, with a mischievous defiance, to do otherwise.

# Here and Now

There are moments in life when we ask ourselves what we truly value. **Would** we sacrifice comfort for the sake of a principle? **Would** we stand firm when everyone around us chooses to look away? These questions don't have easy answers, but they define who we are.

**Here**, in this very place and time, is where our choices matter most. We often dream about some distant future or dwell on the past, forgetting that the present is the only space we can actually influence. Right **here**, right now, we hold the power to make a difference—no matter how small.

Sometimes the bonds that hold us together are thicker than water. **Blood** ties us to family, to heritage, to the generations that came before us. Yet **blood** can also symbolize sacrifice—the effort, sweat, and dedication we pour into the causes we believe in. The **blood** of shared struggle unites strangers into communities and turns ordinary people into heroes.

In the end, the question remains: **would** we, standing **here** today, be willing to give everything—even our own **blood**—for what we hold dear? Perhaps that is the truest measure of a life well lived.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of D.H. Lawrence about eating a peach and contemplating its shape.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Peach**

Would you like to throw a stone at me?
Here, take one.

I have eaten a peach, and now I hold the stone,
this wrinkled, corrugated, blind little pit
that once was the secret heart of all that softness.

Why is it so?
Why is the peach not straight and plain and honest
like an apple, round and public and forthright?

No.
It leans, it curves, it folds itself into a cleft,
a groove running down one side
as though some finger, long ago,
pressed into the wet flesh of the world
and left the mark there, always.

Why the furrow?
Why the blush, the down, the fuzz that shivers
when you bring it to your mouth?
There is nothing accidental in a peach.

It is a thing made in the dark,
in the sap-rising, the sun-swelling,
the slow blind pressure of the summer
pushing sweetness into a curve
that is not the curve of a machine,
not the smooth lie of the manufactured,
but the deep, ripe cleave of living things.

I bit it, and the juice ran down.
Voluptuous, unashamed.
And here is the stone, hard as truth,
still holding the memory of that shape.

So.
Would you like to throw a stone at me?
Go on, then.
I have had my peach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
# What I Hand You

Reader, I have carried this peach
too long in my coat pocket,
letting it bruise against loose change
and the folded receipts of days
I meant to spend more wisely.

Look how it softens
where my thumb kept pressing—
a thing half-ripe, half-ruined,
sweet in patches, sour in others,
the skin gone loose in places
like a promise I couldn't keep taut.

I wanted to give you something round
and whole, something you could bite
without the flesh collapsing,
without the juice running
down your wrist like an apology.

But this is what I grew.
This is the summer I had in me—
uneven, dropped early,
warmed on a windowsill
that never got enough light.

Take it anyway.
Take the parts that give,
the small torn map of my attention,
the taste that isn't finished
becoming what it meant to be.

And when you've eaten
what there is to eat,
when only the hard center remains—

here.

Let me press it into your palm,
this rough and grooved thing,
this knot I couldn't open,
this seed that outlasts
the sweetness it was hiding in.

Plant it, or don't.
I only wanted you to hold
the part of me
that was always going to remain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
